program: Coordinated care, premium assistance, pharmacy and navigation

what: DuPage Health Coalition connects uninsured county residents to primary, specialty and hospital care through a provider network.
It also offers prescription access, insurance premium assistance, health education and benefits or medical debt navigation.
Coordinating care and financial support can help people who face barriers to affordable treatment.
strengths: Original audits identify the enrolled care-access cohort and recipient costs.
Current eligibility and provider arrangements establish an operating mechanism.
Medication and insurance support can protect health and household resources.
reservations: Enrollees are not measured clinical responders or unique households.
Partner resource opportunity costs and actual otherwise-paid savings remain unmeasured.
The broad portfolio and an additional gift's expansion are not captured by a validated causal estimate.

sections.what: DuPage Health Coalition, EIN 36-4448208, serves DuPage County within the Chicago metro. Access DuPage links uninsured residents to low-cost care rather than insurance. Silver Access supports ACA premiums, while pharmacy, education, pantry and navigation programs serve additional needs. The official giving page links a Give Lively route; no checkout transaction was tested.
sections.monitoring: FY2025 audit note 8 identifies 5,871 enrollees, not completed treatments, responders or unique households. The model treats this as an enrolled-cohort proxy; enrollmentFraction=1 is a judgment about annual exposure, with a half-cohort sensitivity. One enrollee per resource household is explicitly judged, not observed. A two-enrollees-per-household sensitivity aggregates both participants' full burdens before the single household log. Annual renewal and treatment uptake are distinct. Track additional completed care, residence, unique households, actual spending, copayments, missed work and alternatives. Cumulative people served since 2001 are not annual outcomes.
sections.qualitative: The previously reviewed Oregon randomized insurance experiment supports access and financial protection as mechanisms but found no significant changes in measured physical endpoints over two years. It is not this coalition's coordinated care or a calibration of its clinical utility, response or spending. Alpha k=.75, a=.25, u=.05 and T=.5 remain explicit unsupported local priors, not an empirically calibrated EV. One finite morbidity area avoids adding referral, prescription and mortality benefits again. A quarter-year delay is now explicit. Other programs retain costs but are unpriced in central clinical benefit because completion, effect and overlap are unknown, not zero or a lower bound.
sections.cost:
FY2025 recipient expense is $4,157,450 including support and $207,956 pantry in-kind already expensed. FY2024 and FY2023 audited recipient expenses are $3,442,757 and $3,122,003; mean $3,574,070. A $4 FY2024 comparative functional-table discrepancy is preserved, with activity-statement amounts used consistently. The April 2025 $1,138,000 building purchase was capitalized; recurring cost retains depreciation rather than adding the entire purchase again. Note 8's over $50 million donated service value is not measured incremental opportunity cost and may overlap recognized resources.

The revised center adds an explicitly unsupported $5 million annual partner opportunity-resource budget, net of overlap with recipient expense, giving $9,157,450. This is a conditional whole annual system-cost hypothesis, not a calibrated economic cost, an actual partner invoice or a mechanical percentage of $50 million retail value. Resource assumptions do not shrink with clinical success or b; the full annual denominator is retained. $1 million/$10 million economic-budget hypotheses, a $50 million reported-value-floor boundary and partner-cost-unknown are separate cases. The legacy recipient-accounting boundary is labeled, not a claim of free partner care. It cannot establish a comparable full-resource rank.

The enrolled proxy × .35 additional annual funded-work response exposes 2,054.85 participant units. Judged .75 treatment and .25 additional clinical response give 385.284375 clinical residents. .05 utility for half a year, quarter-year delay, 3% discount and .99 metro share yield 9.465581 clinical QALYs. b=.35 now denotes a conditional annual-work response beyond substitute funding/capacity, not a second donor haircut on observed incremental outcomes. b=1 is shown; the marginal gift remains unknown.

A distinct .30 resource-success hypothesis gives 616.455 households $300 of medical spending actually otherwise paid within one year, net of insurance, charity assistance, forgone care, taxes, benefits and replacement. This is not retail treatment value. Each positive medical or work component retains .5 for health overlap; negative components remain full. All exposed participants bear a judged $100 incremental time, travel, copay and additional-care burden versus alternatives, including those not clinically treated. The successful household gains $50; 1,438.395 others lose $100. With one welfare-equivalent person per household, $20,000 annual resources and a joint log, the resource component is −2.786380 equivalents. The .30 resource group is not assumed identical to .25 clinical responders. Under household aggregation, costs scale by participants per household before the log; additional family welfare is unpriced.

Combined 6.679202 equivalents imply $13.710396 million per ten combined equivalents, not ten clinical QALYs. The original $4.359839 million recipient-budget health-only price is preserved. The change is an explicit partner-cost hypothesis, delay and signed household ledger, not new demonstrated efficacy or forced favorable change. Clinical-null retains resource exposure and full costs. Separate disjoint ACA-eligible household scenarios model actual premium outflow avoided net of tax credits, member contribution and alternative support, not overlapping insurance-ineligible Access recipients. Debt face value, pantry retail value and ordinary survivor wages are excluded; actual changes in repayment or usable consumption require evidence.

Full enrolled-plus-extra-cohort harm, payer-margin/fiscal incidence and outside own-resource losses are stresses. Payer stresses exclude service inputs already in partner budget; they do not charge the same donated work twice. Positive-only overlap cannot shrink negative components or costs. Central work gain, additional program cohorts and outside incidence are unknown-neutral references, not observed zero or complete world benefit. Full unknown remains distinct from true zero.
sections.funding: The audit reports $4,522,036 operating revenue, $181,919 nonoperating income and $5,574,279 net assets; $4,546,019 financial assets were available within one year. Government and hospital support are substantial, but reserves alone do not prove no useful expansion. Current Access eligibility excludes people eligible for Medicaid, Medicare, ACA or employer insurance; county residence and low income are required. CareLink is Cook-resident restricted and is not assumed available to ordinary DuPage residents. DuPage sliding-fee services, FQHCs, hospital charity care, medication assistance and changing insurance eligibility are relevant alternatives. Silver Access 2026 terms retain tax credits, member premium obligations, copays and deductibles. No priced unfunded capacity, provider expansion commitment or marginal funding replacement was verified. The full portfolio and next-dollar response remain unknown.

model.geographicAttribution: DuPage eligibility anchors local cohort; g=.99 judged. Cook-only CareLink not assumed a DuPage alternative.
model.formula: annual=N*enrollmentFraction; exposed=annual*b; clinical=exposed*k*a; otherExposed=otherHouseholds*b; union=exposed+otherExposed. Q_all=clinical*u*discounted finite years−union*harm/discount(delay); Q_MSA=Q_all*g. Household count=exposed*householdsPerEnrollee; all participant costs aggregate per household before one CG log. Price10=10*(C+partnerCost)/(clinical+signed resources); unknown partner cost gives unknown price.
model.counterfactual: Existing DuPage sliding-fee/FQHC/hospital charity care and insurance alternatives, not Cook-only assistance; some patients otherwise forgo care.
model.attribution: Enrollment exposure, annual funded response, clinical uptake/response and actual resource success are distinct judgments; partner annual costs stay full regardless of clinical success.
model.uncertainty: Conditional reference, not calibrated EV or complete portfolio. Partner opportunity costs, households, local utility, net savings and marginal funding unresolved.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional completed coordinated care, finite morbidity utility and signed actual otherwise-paid medical/premium resources; no debt face value or retail-care income.

historicalAlphaModel.costScope: Full DHC recipient expense, including recorded pantry in-kind; excludes partner care reported above $50m. This is a recipient-budget perspective, not full economic resource cost. The $50m sensitivity is a rounded reported-value floor illustration, not an upper bound or measured opportunity cost.
historicalAlphaModel.counterfactual: a removes equivalent care elsewhere and ineffective care; b separately removes replacement financing/volunteer capacity. One morbidity pathway avoids double counting.
historicalAlphaModel.geographicAttribution: DuPage residence required; .99 allows mobility/errors within the pinned MSA framework.
historicalAlphaModel.uncertainty: Central illustrative scenario and favorable/poor bounds are judgments, not calibrated EV or confidence interval. Cross-recipient results cannot be summed without deduplication. These costs are whole-portfolio equivalents, not marginal gift purchase guarantees. Cost numerators use different accounting recognition of donated care; central prices must not be interpreted as a comparable economic-efficiency ranking. Favorable and poor scenarios are illustrative cases, not exhaustive bounds.
